newsitem.title: GERMANY: Economists see Bundesbank rates on hold -- poll.
newsitem.headline: Economists see Bundesbank rates on hold -- poll.

text.p: The Bundesbank is likely to keep interest rates on hold at its regular council meeting on Thursday and for the rest of the year, economists surveyed by Reuters said unanimously on Tuesday.

All 10 economists who follow the German central bank clsely and were polled by Reuters said they expect interest rates to be unchanged at least until January and that the Bundesbank will adopt another fixed rate securities repurchase agreement, or repo, at the Thursday meeting.
"There is no need to change monetary policy," said Thomas Kull, economist at Westdeutsche Landesbank. "The economy is running OK and monetary policy is already expansive."
About the only chance for any excitement on Thursday could come in a special announcement that the Bundesbank would free repo business from minimum reserve requirements.
But according to the economists, the odds of that happening are slim, only one of the 10 expecting the central bank to make such a move.

Economists said that although recent signals about the economy have not been strong, gross domestic product should start to pick up, leaving the Bundesbank little reason to provide a stimulus through lower interest rates.
"The economy seems to be growing although incoming orders and industrial production are a bit worse," said Ulrich Beckmann, economist at Deutsche Bank. "We expect a slow pick up in the economy."
Others said signs of increasing exports, which have historically been the first part of the economy to expand during an upturn in the business cycle, promise to lift the economy.

Ros Lifton, economist at HSBC Markets, said, for example, she saw no change in interest rates or the tender because the Bundesbank is confident that the correction of the overvalued deutschemark and the decline in long term interest rates will foster the economic recovery.
Several, however, said they thought the Bundesbank was moving toward abolishing the minimum reserve requirement on repos.
The speculation was ignited in early October when Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum told a German newspaper the central bank was likely to free repo business sometime during the autumn.
In Germany, banks must deposit a certain percentage of short-term borrowings from foreign banks and domestic non-banks in non-interest bearing deposits at the Bundesbank.
The minimum reserve requirement is widely seen as a burden which has prompted banks to shift their repurchase business in German securities from Frankfurt to London.
Currently, the level on repo business and sight deposits is two percent, and on savings deposits 1.5 percent.

Under a repo transaction, a dealer borrows funds from an investor by selling securities to him. The dealer repurchases the securities at a later date at a higher price, thereby repaying the loan. The difference between the sale and repurchase price represents interest on the loan.
